title: VaxLedger
description: Search recorded immunizations and export a personal vaccination history with VaxLedger. Review source dates and details without inferring missing doses.
workflow: Search and export authorized immunization history.
subject: Immunization record search & personal export
label: Notes from the register
headline: An immunization history is not a vaccination schedule
summary: Why VaxLedger is a searchable register of returned records, and what to check before using an export.
sections: A register begins with recorded entries

VaxLedger is designed to browse the immunization information supplied in an authorized snapshot. Search helps locate entries and export creates a personal copy. The register does not generate a vaccination plan or determine which vaccines someone needs. Its scope is the recorded history that was actually returned.
Keep the source date in the conversation

An entry’s date and supplied vaccine details help distinguish records that might otherwise look similar. A readable list makes those fields easier to review, but it does not certify that an entry meets a school, travel or employment requirement. Requirements and acceptable evidence belong to the organization requesting them.

An immunization may be absent because a source did not return it or because the selected connection does not cover that part of the record. The app does not label a missing entry as a missed dose. It also does not reconcile all possible sources into a verified universal history. Review coverage warnings and ask the source organization about discrepancies.

VaxLedger’s record adapter is built for FinchNode patient-authorized data. A separate server handles the production credential and temporary sessions; the register displays the authorized result. Live activation is pending, so the deployed code should not be mistaken for evidence that a visitor’s source is already connected.
Use an export as a personal reference

An export records what was available when it was created. It will not receive later corrections or automatically disappear after revocation. Keep it private and review its source context when sharing it deliberately. The ledger helps organize information for a discussion; a care professional or issuing organization must resolve questions about clinical interpretation or official documentation.
guideIntro: Find recorded immunizations, understand what a filtered export includes, and distinguish missing results from a complete vaccination history.
finchnodeContext: VaxLedger uses FinchNode to request the immunization category and displays the returned events as a ledger. Search and JSON export are VaxLedger features; the connection does not turn the ledger into an official certificate or a vaccination schedule.

articles.title: How to search and export immunization records in VaxLedger
articles.description: Filter recorded vaccine entries and export the visible immunization ledger as JSON, with clear limits on what the file establishes.

sections.heading: Search by the displayed vaccine label
paragraphs: The search box filters the labels in the returned immunization list. Start with a short recognizable part of the label and clear the field to restore the full ledger. The entry count describes the current filtered view, not the number of doses in a recommended series.

sections.heading: Read the entry before exporting
paragraphs: Each row presents a label, the available date, source context, status and a code when supplied. These fields describe the returned record. The app does not decide whether an entry meets a school, employment or travel requirement.
items: Check the search field for an active filter.
Review the number of visible entries.
Inspect the source entries if a label or date needs clarification.
Clear the filter if you intend to export every returned immunization.

sections.heading: Know that the export follows the filter
paragraphs: “Export ledger” creates a JSON file containing the rows currently visible after filtering. The file also labels the source and states that it is not for clinical use. A filtered export can intentionally leave out other returned entries, so keep that distinction clear when using the file later.

sections.heading: Check the destination’s requirements separately
paragraphs: A personal JSON export is not an official vaccination certificate. Ask the receiving organization what form of documentation it accepts and obtain source documentation where required. The public site explains the workflow; live authorized imports remain pending activation.

questions.question: Does exporting include hidden search results?
questions.answer: No. VaxLedger exports the filtered rows. Clear the search first to include all returned entries.

questions.question: Can the ledger tell me which vaccination is due?
questions.answer: No. The implemented product organizes recorded history and does not calculate schedules or recommendations.

articles.title: Why a vaccine entry may be missing from your VaxLedger view
articles.description: Separate search filtering, returned source data and authorized categories when investigating a missing immunization entry.

sections.heading: First check whether the view is filtered
paragraphs: A search can hide a record without removing it from the imported data. Clear the vaccine search and compare the entry count. This is the simplest way to distinguish a narrow view from an empty returned ledger.

sections.heading: Then identify the boundary of the imported history
paragraphs: The ledger only contains immunization entries returned to this application. An absent event cannot establish that a person never received a vaccine. Source availability, the selected connection and the information returned for the authorized category define what the app can display.

sections.heading: Use source context to frame the next question
paragraphs: If an expected event is absent, identify which source you expected it to come from and consult that source’s own records. VaxLedger does not search every provider automatically, create replacement entries, or combine personal recollections with imported events.

sections.heading: Do not turn the gap into a schedule
paragraphs: An incomplete ledger is a reason to clarify the documentation, not a basis for the app to recommend a dose. The software deliberately stops at history inspection and export. Future product changes should preserve a visible distinction between source events, user-added notes and any separately validated clinical workflow.

questions.question: Does an empty ledger mean no vaccinations were recorded anywhere?
questions.answer: No. It describes the information available in this app’s current returned view.

questions.question: Can I type in a missing dose?
questions.answer: The current interface has no manual immunization-entry feature.

finchnode.heading: A focused FinchNode request
finchnode.text: VaxLedger’s backend scope is limited to demographics and immunizations through FinchNode. The ledger works with that authorized response rather than treating access to one category as proof of a complete lifetime history.
finchnode.label: FinchNode’s patient-authorized API

articles.title: How to evaluate source coverage for an immunization app
articles.description: VaxLedger offers a practical way to assess returned vaccine history, missing information and export behavior when connecting an independent health product.

sections.heading: Define coverage as a testable question
paragraphs: “Can we connect records?” is too broad to evaluate an immunization product. A more useful question names the source, the approved access path, the category expected and the kind of output the visitor needs. VaxLedger’s current output is a searchable event ledger and a JSON export.

The product does not infer that every lifetime vaccination should be present in one returned category. Evaluation should preserve the distinction between what the connection can return and what the visitor expects to find.

sections.heading: Write down the result before you run the test
paragraphs: For an approved test connection, identify the source context and the available reference documentation. Use an appropriate test environment or a properly authorized live workflow; do not invent a successful patient import from a sample response.

The useful evidence is specific: whether authorization completed, which categories were granted, whether immunization entries were returned and whether their identifying fields survived display and export. A passing network request alone does not establish the quality or completeness of the history.

sections.heading: Where FinchNode fits in the evaluation
paragraphs: VaxLedger uses FinchNode in its source implementation for demographics and immunizations. That defined category scope makes the product’s request easy to explain. The interface then searches and exports the returned immunization entries.

Assess the actual supported source and authorized response, not merely the existence of an integration logo. The site’s current patient connection remains awaiting activation; its public code is an example of the intended request and display boundary.

sections.heading: Include the cases a complete-looking demo can hide
paragraphs: A useful acceptance exercise includes an empty category, a missing date or code, several similarly named events, and a deliberately narrowed search. Check that the app reports the available information without replacing missing fields with invented values.

VaxLedger’s export follows the filtered rows. That means a person can make a partial export even when more events were returned. Include that behavior in the review so a downstream reader does not mistake a filtered file for the complete imported ledger.

sections.heading: Record the boundary as part of the business handoff
paragraphs: When the receiving business enables its own connection, document the tested source path, permission scope and known limitations. Keep the current behavior of the app separate from any future roadmap for broader sources or different exports.

A source-coverage review should make the product easier to explain. It should not turn an event history into a vaccination recommendation or a certificate of eligibility for a particular destination. Those are different claims from the ones this ledger implements.

questions.question: Is a successful connection proof of complete vaccination history?
questions.answer: No. It establishes a successful access path and returned response, whose scope and completeness still need to be understood.

questions.question: Does VaxLedger combine all possible providers automatically?
questions.answer: The app displays the information returned through the authorized connection. It does not establish that every possible provider or historical source was searched.
